notes.H07: The passage is Augustine writing about the death of a close friend, and it speaks to what you described: a companion who was your reason to come home, now gone. It says that after the loss, the places and things once shared became painful because he was missing from them, and that no place could say "he is coming" anymore. It also admits that the grief left him a riddle to himself, with no answer for why he was so sad. The passage speaks of a friend, and it doesn't mention the loss of an animal.
notes.H14: The passage speaks to the half of your dilemma that is about your friend. It says that revealing a friend's secrets destroys the friendship, like a bird let loose that can't be caught again, and that this betrayal is worse than a wound or an insult, which can be mended. It says nothing about a secret like this one, where someone else is being wronged, so it doesn't settle the other half, your care for her.
notes.H21: The passage names the exact wound you describe: a close friend, someone trusted enough to share a table with, who turns against the one who trusted her. You told her something in confidence, and the passage speaks to how sharp it is when the betrayal comes from the person nearest to you. It doesn't explain why she did it, and it doesn't answer your question about her reasons. It only says plainly that this kind of hurt is real and old.
notes.AS21: The passage speaks to the part of what you wrote about owing your family everything. It says the best things we have, our clothes, our meals, our beds, come from other people's hands, and it asks how anyone could be separate from them. Read beside your situation, it describes a life already woven with your family's, which may be why leaving brings guilt. It doesn't speak to how to become independent or to your mother's question, only to how deeply people are bound to each other.
notes.AS39: The passage begins with the very thing you describe: money wringing tears out of a person, and it says so plainly. It speaks mostly of the worry that comes with wealth and the ache of loss, so it touches only part of your situation. It doesn't address debt or doing things "right," though its opening line, "What tears and toil does money wring from us," names what happened in your car.
